Primary control: Per-invocation JSONL records from every hook; daily S3 upload with Object Lock (GOVERNANCE, 395-day WORM); write-only device writer and separate read-only investigator identity
Main risk addressed: Repudiation; log tampering; undetected policy evasion
ISO 42001 / NIST AI RMF alignment: ISO 42001 monitoring and records control; NIST Measure and Govern
Implementation notes: Each hook appends an allow/deny/redact/observe record via lib/audit-log.sh. Logs rotate locally and ship off-box daily; WORM retention prevents post-hoc deletion. Note the audit trail is per top-level command only: subprocess-spawning tools log one line and do not record what they spawn (see command allowlist governance).
Threat vector: Agent or compromised session acting without an attributable, immutable record
Claude Code manifestation: Denied/allowed actions not captured or logs altered to hide misuse
Organizational impact: High: Loss of forensic evidence and accountability

Primary control: Default-deny Bash allowlist in bash-policy-check.sh; scoped read-only entries; subprocess-spawning commands excluded pending recorded decision

Implementation notes: Allowlist changes are paired in-PR with behavioural tests (test-guardrails SKILL.md), an offline harness (run-bash-policy-tests.sh), and a risk decision log (docs/command-allowlist-risk-assessment.md). Commands that spawn subprocesses (make, gradle, npx, docker compose up) bypass the per-command hook and are contained only by the OS sandbox, so they require an explicit policy decision, not a config tweak.
Threat vector: Allowlisting a spawner or mis-scoped verb that executes arbitrary project-defined code
Claude Code manifestation: Agent runs unreviewed code via a build/test wrapper the hook cannot inspect
Organizational impact: Moderate: Sandbox becomes the sole control and the audit trail loses per-subprocess visibility
